content: Module 1: Introduction to Multimedia Systems A Multimedia System is a system capable of processing multimedia data and applications. It is characterized by the processing, storage, generation, manipulation, and rendition of multimedia information.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: 1.1 Four Basic Characteristics of Multimedia Systems Computer-Controlled: Systems must be managed and controlled by computing architecture. Integrated: Different media types are combined into a cohesive presentation. Digital Representation: The information handled must be represented in digital form. Interactive Presentation: The interface to the final presentation of media typically allows user interaction.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: Module 2: Desirable Features for a Multimedia System Very High Processing Power: Essential for large data processing and real-time delivery of media. Special hardware is commonplace. Multimedia Capable File System: Needed to deliver real-time media such as video and audio streaming (e.g., RAID technology). Efficient and High I/O: Input and output to the file subsystem need to be extremely fast and efficient, supporting real-time recording and playback (e.g., Direct-to-Disk recording). Special Operating Systems: Must support direct transfers to disk, real-time scheduling, fast interrupt processing, and I/O streaming. Storage and Memory: Large storage units ($\ge 50-100\text{ GB}$) and large memory ($\ge 50-100\text{ MB}$), accompanied by Level 2 and Level 3 cache hierarchies. Network Support: Distributed client-server systems are standard. Software Tools: User-friendly tools to handle media, design applications, and deliver content.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: Module 3: Components of a Multimedia System Capture Devices: Video cameras, recorders, microphones, keyboards, mice, graphics tablets, 3D input devices, tactile sensors, and VR equipment. Digitizing / Sampling Hardware: Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). Storage Devices: Hard disks, CD-ROMs, Jaz/Zip drives, DVDs. Communication Networks: Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI, ATM, Intranets, Internets. Computer Systems: Multimedia desktop machines, workstations, MPEG/Video/DSP hardware. Display Devices: CD-quality speakers, HDTV, SVGA, high-resolution monitors, color printers.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: Module 4: Media Types & Signal Technology Static or Discrete Media: Time-independent media (e.g., standard text, single images, graphics). Continuous Media: Time-dependent media with temporal relationships (e.g., video, animation, audio).
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: 4.1 Analog vs. Digital Signals Analog Signals: Continuous time signals represented by sinusoidal waveforms where amplitude varies continuously with time (used for sound, temperature, and light). Digital Signals: Finite number of discrete values limited to binary values ($0$ or $1$). Offers high accuracy, processing speed, and noise immunity. Conversion: Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC): Converts continuous analog signals into discrete digital signals. Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC): Performs the converse operation for playback.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: Quick Study Summary Checklist Four characteristics: Computer-controlled, integrated, digital representation, interactive. Hardware needs: High processing power, RAID, high I/O, L2/L3 caches. Media classification: Discrete (text/images) vs. Continuous (video/audio). Conversion: ADC for input digitizing, DAC for output playback.
title: Mastering Multimedia Systems & Signals (Lecture 02)

content: Academic Note: This master study guide covers Chapter 1 (“Introduction to Multimedia”) of Fundamentals of Multimedia (3rd Edition) by Ze-Nian Li, Mark S. Drew, and Jiangchuan Liu.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: Module 1: What is Multimedia? Depending on who you ask, the term “multimedia” has different viewpoints: Consumer Entertainment Vendor: Interactive TV with hundreds of digital channels, cable-like services over high-speed internet, or a smartphone. Computer Science (CS) Student / Researcher: Applications that use multiple modalities, including text, images, drawings (graphics), animation, video, sound (including speech), and interactivity.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 1.1 Formal Definition General Definition: Multimedia is the field concerned with the computer-controlled integration of text, graphics, drawings, still and moving images (video), animation, audio, and any other media where every type of information can be represented, stored, transmitted, and processed digitally. Multimedia Application: An application that uses a collection of multiple media sources (e.g., text, graphics, images, sound/audio, animation, and/or video).
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 1.2 Components of Multimedia (Modalities) Multimedia involves multiple modalities put to use in various advanced systems: Video-conferencing & Tele-medicine. Cloud-based web video editors for editing and remixing professional videos. Real-time augmented reality (AR) and massively multiplayer online video games. Shapeshifting TV (viewers vote on plot paths) and inverse-Hollywood applications. Large-scale video/image database semantic searching. Hybrid compositing of artificial and natural video.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: Module 2: Multimedia Research Topics & Interdisciplinary Nature To computer scientists, multimedia research spans three major pillars: Multimedia Processing and Coding: Content analysis, content-based retrieval, security, audio/image/video processing, and compression. Multimedia System Support and Networking: Network protocols, the Internet, operating systems, servers/clients, Quality of Service (QoS), and databases. Multimedia Tools, End-Systems, and Applications: Hypermedia systems, user interfaces, authoring systems, multimodal interaction, “ubiquity” (web-everywhere devices), and virtual environments.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 2.1 Interdisciplinary Connections Electrical Engineering: Signal processing for audio/video signals. Physics: Color science in images and video. Medicine & Psychology: Human perception of multimedia data.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: Module 3: Multimedia: Past and Present
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 3.1 Early History (Analog Era) All early mass communication media were in analog format, where the time-varying signal feature is a continuous representation (analogous) to the input signal: Newspaper (Text, graphics, images): Perhaps the first mass communication medium. Motion Pictures (1830s): Conceived to observe motion too rapid for perception by the human eye. Wireless Radio Transmission (1895): Guglielmo Marconi in Pontecchio, Italy. Television (20th Century): Established video as a widely available mass medium. Note on Audio Storage: Evolved from Edison’s 1877 phonograph cylinder to flat vinyl records, reel-to-reel magnetic tape, cassette tapes, and compact discs (CDs).
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 3.2 Hypermedia, WWW, and Internet Timeline 1945: Vannevar Bush wrote a landmark article describing Memex (early hypermedia). 1965: Ted Nelson coined the term hypertext (non-linear text containing links). 1968: Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the On-Line System (NLS). 1989: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web (WWW). 1991: MPEG-1 approved; introduction of PDAs. 1992: JPEG image compression standard accepted. 1993: NCSA Mosaic released (first full-fledged web browser). 1995: Java language created for platform-independent development. 1996: DVD video introduced.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 3.3 Linear vs. Non-Linear Presentation Linear Presentation: Progresses without navigational control for the viewer (e.g., cinema). Non-Linear / Interactive: Uses interactivity to control progress (e.g., video games, hypermedia).
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: 3.4 Markup Languages HTML (HyperText Markup Language): Published via ASCII for portability across hardware architectures (Current standard: HTML5). XML (Extensible Markup Language): Separates data structure and view, allowing users/applications to define custom tags.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: Module 4: Multimedia in the New Millennium (2000–Present) 2004: Web 2.0 promotes user collaboration (Facebook, Flickr founded). 2005: YouTube created; Google Maps launched. 2006: Twitter created; Amazon cloud computing launched; Nintendo Wii released (3D movement detection). 2007: Apple iPhone (iOS) and Google Android launched. 2010: Netflix migrates to cloud; Microsoft Kinect introduced (3D motion & voice capture). 2013: 4K TVs available; YouTube supports 360-degree videos; AlphaGo beats human professional. 2016: Microsoft HoloLens (mixed reality); Pokémon Go popularizes AR. 2018: 16K Ultra HD video; 5G deployment; Wi-Fi 6 released. 2020: COVID-19 pandemic drives booming remote work/study tools (Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Classroom).
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

content: Module 5: Multimedia Software Tools Core software tools used in multimedia development include: Music sequencing and notation software. Digital audio editors. Graphics and image editing suites. Video editing software. Animation tools. Multimedia authoring and broadcasting systems.
title: Introduction to Multimedia: Fundamentals & History (CO1224 Lecture 01)

Understand the 3 main CS research pillars: Processing/Coding, Systems/Networking, and Tools/Applications. Distinguish between analog media (continuous representation) and digital media (binary format). Explain the difference between linear presentations (cinema) and non-linear/interactive presentations (games, hype rmedia). Know the historical milestones: Ted Nelson (Hypertext, 1965), Tim Berners-Lee (WWW, 1989), and NCSA Mosaic (1993).

content: Academic Note: This master study guide focuses on advanced Data Definition Language (DDL) concepts, exploring robust table creation techniques, relational constraint enforcement, and schema modifications using the ALTER TABLE statement.
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: Module 1: Core Table Creation Techniques & Key Syntaxes When designing a relational database, enforcing data integrity through keys is crucial. Keys dictate how rows are uniquely identified and how tables relate to one another.
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 1.1 Column-Level vs. Table-Level Constraints Column-Level Constraints: Applied directly inline after a column’s data type (best for simple single-column keys). Table-Level Constraints: Defined at the bottom of the CREATE TABLE statement (mandatory for composite keys consisting of two or more columns).
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 1.2 Primary Key (PRIMARY KEY) A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table. It cannot contain NULL values, and all values must be unique. Example (Column-Level): CREATE TABLE Guest ( GuestNo INT PRIMARY KEY, GuestName VARCHAR(50) );Example (Table-Level): CREATE TABLE Guest ( GuestNo INT, GuestName VARCHAR(50), CONSTRAINT pk_guest PRIMARY KEY (GuestNo) );
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 1.3 Composite Primary Keys When a single column is insufficient to uniquely identify a row, a combination of two or more columns forms a composite primary key. (As seen in Lecture 08 with Room and Booking tables). Syntax Example: CREATE TABLE Room ( RoomNo INT, HotelNo VARCHAR(10), Type VARCHAR(20), Price DECIMAL(6,2), PRIMARY KEY (RoomNo, HotelNo) );
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 1.4 Foreign Key (FOREIGN KEY) A foreign key is a field (or collection of fields) in one table that references a key in another table, establishing a parent-child relationship and ensuring referential integrity. Syntax Example: CREATE TABLE Booking ( HotelNo VARCHAR(10), GuestNo INT, DateFrom DATE, RoomNo INT, PRIMARY KEY (HotelNo, GuestNo, DateFrom), FOREIGN KEY (HotelNo) REFERENCES Hotel(HotelNo), FOREIGN KEY (GuestNo) REFERENCES Guest(GuestNo) );
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: Module 2: Modifying Existing Tables Using ALTER TABLE The ALTER TABLE statement is used to add, delete, or modify columns and constraints in an existing table without dropping and recreating it.
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.1 Adding a New Column (ADD COLUMN) To add a new column (e.g., email to the Guest table): ALTER TABLE Guest ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100);
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.2 Dropping a Column (DROP COLUMN) To remove an unwanted column from a table: ALTER TABLE Guest DROP COLUMN email;
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.3 Modifying Column Data Types (MODIFY or CHANGE) To change a column’s data type or constraints: ALTER TABLE Guest MODIFY COLUMN GuestName VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL;
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.4 Adding a Primary Key Constraint via ALTER If a table was created without a primary key, you can add it afterward: ALTER TABLE students ADD PRIMARY KEY (index_no);
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.5 Adding a Foreign Key Constraint via ALTER To establish a foreign key relationship on an existing table: ALTER TABLE Room ADD CONSTRAINT fk_hotel_room FOREIGN KEY (HotelNo) REFERENCES Hotel(HotelNo);
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: 2.6 Dropping Constraints (DROP FOREIGN KEY / DROP PRIMARY KEY) To remove a foreign key constraint, you usually reference its constraint name: ALTER TABLE Room DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_hotel_room;To remove a primary key: ALTER TABLE students DROP PRIMARY KEY;
title: Advanced Table Creation, Constraints, and the ALTER Statement (SQL Master Guide)

content: Quick Study Summary Checklist Primary key rule: Must be unique and cannot contain NULL. Composite key rule: Must be defined at the table-level when using multiple columns. Foreign key rule: Links child table columns to parent table keys to maintain referential integrity. ALTER TABLE ADD: Used to insert new columns or apply constraints post-creation. ALTER TABLE DROP: Used to remove columns or constraints safely. ALTER TABLE MODIFY: Used to update data types or column rules. title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: MySQL Identity & Pronunciation MySQL is pronounced “my Ess Que Ell”. MySQL is an open-source Relational Database Management System (RDBMS).
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Authentication For a default local MySQL root-user installation, login may require no password. If the prompt asks for a password and your installation has none configured, simply press Enter.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Syntax Rules Every SQL command must end with a semicolon (;) or \g. SQL keywords are case-insensitive. For example, SELECT and select are equivalent. Multi-line commands use the -> continuation prompt. Abort an ongoing command using \c.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Essential Diagnostic Commands SELECT VERSION(), CURRENT_DATE; SELECT SIN(PI()/4), (4+1)*5; QUIT;SELECT VERSION(), CURRENT_DATE; displays the MySQL version and current date. SELECT SIN(PI()/4), (4+1)*5; demonstrates that MySQL can also perform mathematical calculations. QUIT; exits the MySQL client. You can also use: exit;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 2: Databases & Table Schemas (Lecture 04)
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Database Management List all available databases: SHOW DATABASES;Create a database: CREATE DATABASE tceusl;Select the database you want to work with: USE tceusl;List the tables inside the current database: SHOW TABLES;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Table Creation & Data Types Create a students table: CREATE TABLE students ( index_no VARCHAR(20), fname VARCHAR(20), lname VARCHAR(20), address VARCHAR(30), sex CHAR(1), birth_date DATE, dept VARCHAR(5), campus VARCHAR(5), tp_no VARCHAR(15) );
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Schema Inspection Use DESCRIBE to inspect the structure of a table: DESCRIBE students;You can also use: DESC students;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Table Deletion To permanently delete a table: DROP TABLE students;Warning: DROP TABLE removes the table structure and its data.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Data Insertion Insert a single row using: INSERT INTO students VALUES ( '001', 'Barath', 'Perera', 'Colombo', 'm', '1995-05-10', 'COM', 'CMB', '0712345678' );You can also explicitly specify the columns: INSERT INTO students (index_no, fname, lname, address, sex, birth_date, dept, campus, tp_no) VALUES ('001', 'Barath', 'Perera', 'Colombo', 'm', '1995-05-10', 'COM', 'CMB', '0712345678');For bulk data import, MySQL can use: LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 'students.csv' INTO TABLE students FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' LINES TERMINATED BY '\n';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 3: Data Retrieval & Filtering (Lecture 05)
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: The Core SELECT Format The basic structure of a query is: SELECT what_to_select FROM which_table WHERE conditions;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Selecting All Columns To retrieve every column and every row: SELECT * FROM students;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Exact Matching Find students whose first name is exactly Barath: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname = 'Barath';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Comparison Operators SQL supports common comparison operators: Operator Meaning = Equal to <> Not equal to != Not equal to > Greater than < Less than >= Greater than or equal to <= Less than or equal to Example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE birth_date >= '1991-01-01';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Logical AND Both conditions must be true: SELECT * FROM students WHERE dept = 'PHY' AND sex = 'f';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Logical OR At least one condition must be true: SELECT * FROM students WHERE sex = 'f' OR dept = 'COM';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Column Projection You do not need to retrieve every column. Specify only the columns you need: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students;This is called projection.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 4: Sorting & NULL Handling (Lecture 06)
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Result Ordering with ORDER BY Sort students by birth date in ascending order: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY birth_date;Ascending order is the default. You can also write: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY birth_date ASC;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Descending Order To sort from newest to oldest: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY birth_date DESC;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Sorting by Multiple Columns You can sort using more than one column: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY dept ASC, birth_date DESC;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Handling NULL NULL represents a missing, unknown, or unavailable value. Never use = to test for NULL. Incorrect: WHERE tp_no = NULL;Correct: SELECT fname FROM students WHERE tp_no IS NULL;To find rows where the phone number is available: SELECT fname FROM students WHERE tp_no IS NOT NULL;Remember: IS NULL → value is missing/unknown. IS NOT NULL → value exists/is not NULL.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 5: Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: LIKE Pattern Matching The LIKE operator is used for standard SQL pattern matching.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: % Wildcard % matches zero or more arbitrary characters. Find names beginning with M: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE 'M%';Find names ending with na: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '%na';Find names containing ar: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '%ar%';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: _ Wildcard _ matches exactly one character. For example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '______';This matches names containing exactly six characters.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Regular Expressions with REGEXP MySQL also supports regular-expression pattern matching through REGEXP. Find names beginning with M: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname REGEXP '^M';Find names ending with a: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname REGEXP 'a$';Find names containing exactly six characters: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname REGEXP '^.{6}$';
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Important Regular Expression Symbols Symbol Meaning ^ Start of string $ End of string . Any single character * Zero or more occurrences + One or more occurrences
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 6: Multiple Tables & Relational Design (Lecture 08)
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Primary Keys A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table. Example: CREATE TABLE students ( index_no VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, fname VARCHAR(20), lname VARCHAR(20) );A primary key: Must uniquely identify each row. Cannot contain duplicate values. Cannot contain NULL values.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Foreign Keys A foreign key creates a relationship between tables. Example: CREATE TABLE departments ( dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_name VARCHAR(50) );A student table can reference the department: CREATE TABLE students ( index_no VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, fname VARCHAR(20), dept_id INT, FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES departments(dept_id) );
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Composite Primary Keys A composite primary key consists of two or more columns. Example: CREATE TABLE enrollment ( student_id INT, course_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id) );Together, student_id and course_id uniquely identify a record.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Aggregate Functions Aggregate functions perform calculations over multiple rows. COUNT() SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;AVG() SELECT AVG(price) FROM products;SUM() SELECT SUM(price) FROM products;Common aggregate functions include: COUNT() — counts rows/values. AVG() — calculates an average. SUM() — calculates a total. MIN() — finds the smallest value. MAX() — finds the largest value.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Part 7: SQL Joins (Lecture 09) Joins allow data from multiple related tables to be retrieved in a single query.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Equi-Join vs Non-Equi-Join An equi-join uses the equality operator (=) to match rows. SELECT * FROM students s JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;A non-equi-join uses comparison operators such as >, <, >=, or <=. SELECT * FROM employees e JOIN salary_grades g ON e.salary >= g.min_salary AND e.salary <= g.max_salary;
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: INNER JOIN An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have matching values in both tables. SELECT * FROM students s INNER JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;INNER JOIN = Only matching rows from both tables.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: LEFT JOIN A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table. SELECT * FROM students s LEFT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;If no match exists, the right-side columns contain NULL. LEFT JOIN = Keep all rows from the left table.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: RIGHT JOIN A RIGHT JOIN returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table. SELECT * FROM students s RIGHT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;RIGHT JOIN = Keep all rows from the right table.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: FULL OUTER JOIN A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all matching and non-matching rows from both tables. Standard SQL syntax: SELECT * FROM table_A FULL OUTER JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;MySQL Note: MySQL does not directly support FULL OUTER JOIN. It can be simulated using LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and UNION. SELECT * FROM table_A LEFT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A UNION SELECT * FROM table_A RIGHT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;FULL OUTER JOIN = Keep all rows from both tables.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: NATURAL JOIN A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins tables using compatible columns with the same names. SELECT * FROM students NATURAL JOIN departments;No explicit ON clause is required. Caution: NATURAL JOIN can produce unexpected results if tables contain multiple identically named columns. Explicit JOIN ... ON ... syntax is usually clearer and safer.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: CROSS JOIN A CROSS JOIN generates a Cartesian product. If Table A has 5 rows and Table B has 3 rows: 5 × 3 = 15 rowsExample: SELECT * FROM students CROSS JOIN courses;CROSS JOIN = Every possible combination of rows.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: SELF JOIN A self join joins a table with itself. Example: SELECT e.employee_name AS employee, m.employee_name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;Here: e = employee m = managerSELF JOIN = A table joined with itself.
title: The Ultimate Master Summary Guide: MySQL & SQL Fundamentals (Lectures 03–09)

content: Module 1: What is an SQL Join? A JOIN clause is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them, creating a temporary result set of rows. Joins are one of the most important concepts in relational databases because information is normally distributed across multiple related tables.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 1.1 Why Are Joins Needed? Consider a hotel database containing separate tables such as: Hotel Room Guest Booking The Hotel table may contain hotel information, while the Room table contains room information. To display a hotel name together with its rooms, information from both tables must be combined. For example: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;The JOIN operation allows related records from different tables to be displayed together.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 1.2 Classifications of Joins SQL joins can be classified according to the condition used to match rows. EQUI JOIN An Equi-Join uses the equality operator (=) as the comparison operator. Example: SELECT * FROM Hotel JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;The rows are matched when: Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNoNON-EQUI JOIN A Non-Equi-Join uses comparison operators other than =. Examples include: > < >= <= <> Example: SELECT * FROM Room R1 JOIN Room R2 ON R1.Price > R2.Price;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 2: Complete List of SQL Joins The major SQL join types are: INNER JOIN LEFT JOIN RIGHT JOIN FULL OUTER JOIN NATURAL JOIN CROSS JOIN SELF JOIN The following sections explain each type in detail.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 3: INNER JOIN An INNER JOIN returns only rows where a matching record exists in both tables.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 3.1 Definition An Inner Join compares related columns from two tables and returns only the matching records. If a record exists in the first table but has no matching record in the second table, it is excluded from the result.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 3.2 General Syntax SELECT columns FROM table_A INNER JOIN table_B ON table_A.column = table_B.column;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 3.3 Basic Example SELECT * FROM table_A INNER JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 3.4 Hotel Database Example To display hotel names together with their rooms: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Room.Price FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This query returns only hotels that have matching records in the Room table.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 3.5 Important Rule INNER JOIN = Return only matching rows from both tables.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 4: LEFT JOIN A LEFT JOIN, also called a LEFT OUTER JOIN, returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If no matching row exists in the right table, the right-side columns contain NULL.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 4.1 General Syntax SELECT columns FROM table_A LEFT JOIN table_B ON table_A.column = table_B.column;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 4.2 Example SELECT * FROM table_A LEFT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 4.3 Hotel Example To display all hotels, including hotels that do not currently have rooms: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type FROM Hotel LEFT JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This is particularly useful when you want to preserve every record from the left table.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 4.4 Important Rule LEFT JOIN = Keep all rows from the left table. If there is no matching record on the right: Right-side columns = NULL
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 5: RIGHT JOIN A RIGHT JOIN, also called a RIGHT OUTER JOIN, returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table. If there is no matching row in the left table, the left-side columns contain NULL.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 5.1 General Syntax SELECT columns FROM table_A RIGHT JOIN table_B ON table_A.column = table_B.column;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 5.2 Example SELECT * FROM table_A RIGHT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 5.3 Hotel Example SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type FROM Hotel RIGHT JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This query preserves every row from the Room table.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 5.4 Important Rule RIGHT JOIN = Keep all rows from the right table.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 6: FULL OUTER JOIN A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all matching and non-matching rows from both tables. It combines the behavior of: LEFT JOIN RIGHT JOIN
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 6.1 Concept A Full Outer Join returns: Matching rows + Unmatched rows from the left table + Unmatched rows from the right tableMissing values are represented by NULL.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 6.2 Standard SQL Syntax SELECT * FROM table_A FULL OUTER JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 6.3 Important MySQL Note MySQL does not directly support the FULL OUTER JOIN syntax. A Full Outer Join can instead be simulated using LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and UNION. Example: SELECT * FROM table_A LEFT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A UNION SELECT * FROM table_A RIGHT JOIN table_B ON table_A.A = table_B.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 6.4 Important Rule FULL OUTER JOIN = Keep all rows from both tables.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 7: NATURAL JOIN A NATURAL JOIN is a special type of Equi-Join. It automatically matches columns that have the same name in both tables.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 7.1 Definition A Natural Join automatically identifies columns with matching names and compatible data types. For example, if both tables contain: HotelNoMySQL can automatically use that column as the joining condition.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 7.2 Syntax SELECT * FROM table_A NATURAL JOIN table_B;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 7.3 Hotel Example SELECT * FROM Hotel NATURAL JOIN Room;If both tables contain a compatible column called HotelNo, MySQL automatically uses it to establish the relationship.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 7.4 Important Rule Do not use an ON clause with a Natural Join. Correct: SELECT * FROM Hotel NATURAL JOIN Room;Incorrect: SELECT * FROM Hotel NATURAL JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 7.5 Important Warning Natural Joins should be used carefully because adding another column with the same name to either table can change the automatic joining behavior.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 8: CROSS JOIN A CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product. Every row from the first table is combined with every row from the second table.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.1 Definition If: Table A = 5 rows Table B = 4 rowsthen: CROSS JOIN result = 5 × 4 = 20 rows
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.2 Syntax SELECT * FROM table_A CROSS JOIN table_B;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.3 Example SELECT * FROM Hotel CROSS JOIN Room;Every hotel is combined with every room record.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.4 Cartesian Product Formula Number of result rows = Rows in Table A × Rows in Table B
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.5 CROSS JOIN with WHERE A Cross Join can be combined with a WHERE condition. For example: SELECT * FROM Hotel, Room WHERE Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This produces results similar to an Inner Join.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 8.6 Important Rule CROSS JOIN = Every row from Table A × Every row from Table B.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 9: SELF JOIN A SELF JOIN occurs when a table is joined with itself. The same table is treated as two separate logical instances by using aliases.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 9.1 Why Use a Self Join? Self Joins are useful when records within the same table have relationships with other records in that same table. Common examples include: Employee and manager relationships Parent and child relationships Hierarchical structures Comparing records within the same table
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 9.2 Basic Syntax SELECT * FROM table_A X JOIN table_A Y ON X.A = Y.A;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 9.3 Example SELECT * FROM table_A X, table_A Y WHERE X.A = Y.A;Here: X = first logical copy of table_A Y = second logical copy of table_A
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 9.4 Employee Example Suppose an employee table contains: EmployeeID EmployeeName ManagerIDA Self Join can be used to display employees and their managers: SELECT E.EmployeeName AS Employee, M.EmployeeName AS Manager FROM Employee E LEFT JOIN Employee M ON E.ManagerID = M.EmployeeID;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 11: Practical Hotel Database Join Queries The following examples demonstrate how joins can be applied to the hotel database.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.1 Display Hotels and Their Rooms SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Room.Price FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This displays only hotels that have corresponding room records.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.2 Display All Hotels Including Hotels Without Rooms Use a LEFT JOIN: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type FROM Hotel LEFT JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;This ensures that hotels without rooms are still displayed. Their room-related columns will contain: NULL
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.3 Display All Rooms with Their Hotel Names SELECT Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Room.Price, Hotel.HotelName FROM Room INNER JOIN Hotel ON Room.HotelNo = Hotel.HotelNo;This combines room information with the corresponding hotel name.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.4 Display Guests and Their Bookings To display guests together with their booking information: SELECT Guest.GuestName, Booking.HotelNo, Booking.RoomNo, Booking.DateFrom, Booking.DateTo FROM Guest INNER JOIN Booking ON Guest.GuestNo = Booking.GuestNo;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.5 Display Booking Information with Hotel Names SELECT Guest.GuestName, Hotel.HotelName, Booking.RoomNo, Booking.DateFrom, Booking.DateTo FROM Booking INNER JOIN Guest ON Booking.GuestNo = Guest.GuestNo INNER JOIN Hotel ON Booking.HotelNo = Hotel.HotelNo;This query combines information from three tables: Booking ↓ Guest ↓ Hotel
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.6 Display Room Information with Hotel and City SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Hotel.City, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Room.Price FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 11.7 Display All Hotels and Their Available Rooms SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Hotel.City, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Room.Price FROM Hotel LEFT JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo ORDER BY Hotel.HotelName;
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 12: Joining Multiple Tables SQL allows more than two tables to be joined in a single query. For example, the hotel database can connect: Hotel ↓ Room Hotel ↓ Booking ↓ Guest
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 12.1 Three-Table Join SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Guest.GuestName, Booking.RoomNo, Booking.DateFrom, Booking.DateTo FROM Booking INNER JOIN Hotel ON Booking.HotelNo = Hotel.HotelNo INNER JOIN Guest ON Booking.GuestNo = Guest.GuestNo;This query combines: Booking Hotel Guest
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 12.2 Four-Table Join To combine all four hotel database tables: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Type, Guest.GuestName, Booking.DateFrom, Booking.DateTo FROM Booking INNER JOIN Hotel ON Booking.HotelNo = Hotel.HotelNo INNER JOIN Room ON Booking.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo AND Booking.RoomNo = Room.RoomNo INNER JOIN Guest ON Booking.GuestNo = Guest.GuestNo;This demonstrates how multiple relationships can be used in one query.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 13: JOIN Conditions and the ON Clause The ON clause specifies how two tables are related. Example: SELECT * FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;The condition: Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNotells MySQL which records should be matched.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: 13.1 Why Is ON Important? Without an appropriate join condition, the query may produce incorrect results or a Cartesian product. Always identify the relationship between the tables before writing the Join condition.
title: SQL Joins: Comprehensive Guide to Combining Tables (Lecture 09)

content: Module 14: Table Aliases Table aliases make complex Join queries shorter and easier to read. Instead of: SELECT Hotel.HotelName, Room.RoomNo, Room.Price FROM Hotel INNER JOIN Room ON Hotel.HotelNo = Room.HotelNo;we can write: SELECT H.HotelName, R.RoomNo, R.Price FROM Hotel H INNER JOIN Room R ON H.HotelNo = R.HotelNo;Here: H = Hotel R = Room

content: Module 18: Join Selection Guide Use an INNER JOIN when: You only want matching records. Use a LEFT JOIN when: You want every record from the left table, even when no match exists. Use a RIGHT JOIN when: You want every record from the right table, even when no match exists. Use a FULL OUTER JOIN when: You want every record from both tables. Use a NATURAL JOIN when: Tables have appropriately named common columns and automatic matching is desired. Use a CROSS JOIN when: You intentionally need every possible combination of rows. Use a SELF JOIN when: A table needs to be compared or related to itself.

content: Module 1: Introduction to Relational Database Design A relational database organizes information into multiple tables that are connected through relationships. Instead of storing all information in one large table, related information is separated into different tables. For the hotel management system, the database contains four main tables: Hotel — Stores information about hotels. Room — Stores information about rooms belonging to hotels. Guest — Stores information about hotel guests. Booking — Stores information about room bookings. The relationships between these tables are established using primary keys and foreign keys.

content: Module 3: Primary Keys A primary key is a column, or combination of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in a table. A primary key: Must uniquely identify records. Cannot contain duplicate values. Cannot contain NULL values. Helps establish relationships between tables.

content: Module 4: Composite Primary Keys A composite primary key consists of two or more columns. The Room table uses: RoomNo + HotelNoas its composite primary key. This is necessary because the same room number can exist in different hotels. For example: RoomNo = 1001, HotelNo = ch01 RoomNo = 1001, HotelNo = dc01 RoomNo = 1001, HotelNo = fb02Although the RoomNo is the same, the combination of RoomNo and HotelNo is unique. The table definition is: CREATE TABLE Room ( RoomNo INT, HotelNo VARCHAR(10), Type VARCHAR(20), Price DECIMAL(6,2), PRIMARY KEY (RoomNo, HotelNo) );

content: Module 5: Foreign Keys A foreign key is a column that refers to a primary key in another table. Foreign keys establish relationships between tables. content: Module 1: Overview of Pattern Matching in MySQL MySQL provides two primary approaches for matching patterns within string data: Standard SQL Pattern Matching using the LIKE operator and wildcards. Regular Expression Pattern Matching using the REGEXP operator. Pattern matching is useful when you want to search for records based on partial text instead of requiring an exact match. For example, instead of searching for one specific name: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname = 'Mohan';you can search for names that begin with, end with, or contain particular characters.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: Module 2: Standard SQL Pattern Matching with LIKE The LIKE operator is used to compare a string against a specified pattern. MySQL provides two important wildcards for LIKE: % (Percent sign): Matches zero or more characters. _ (Underscore): Matches exactly one character.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: 2.1 General Syntax SELECT columns FROM table_name WHERE column_name LIKE 'pattern';
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: 2.2 Finding Names Beginning with a Specific Letter To display all student records where the first name begins with the letter M: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE 'M%';The pattern: M%means: M + zero or more charactersTherefore, names such as: Mohan Malith Mithujancan match the pattern if they exist in the table.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: 2.3 Finding Names Ending with Specific Characters To display all student records where the first name ends with na: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '%na';The pattern: %nameans: zero or more characters + na
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: 2.4 Finding Names Containing Specific Characters To find names containing an anywhere in the string: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '%an%';The % wildcard can appear before and after the search text.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: Module 3: The % Wildcard The percent sign % represents zero or more characters. For example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE 'M%';The pattern can match: M Mohan Malith Mithujandepending on the actual data.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: Important Rule % = zero or more charactersTherefore: M%means the string must begin with M, but there is no restriction on how many characters follow it.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: Module 4: The _ Wildcard The underscore _ represents exactly one character. For example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '_ohan';The pattern: _ohanmeans: one character + ohanTherefore, a five-character value such as: Mohancan match the pattern.
title: SQL Pattern Matching & Regular Expressions (Lecture 07)

content: 4.1 Matching Exactly Six Characters To find names containing exactly six characters, use six underscore characters: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname LIKE '______';The six underscores represent: _ _ _ _ _ _ 1 2 3 4 5 6Therefore: ______ = exactly six characters

content: 8.1 Caret (^) The caret ^ represents the beginning of a string. Example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname REGEXP '^M';The pattern: ^Mmeans: The string must begin with M.

content: Module 10: Matching Exact Lengths with REGEXP Regular expressions can also be used to match strings containing an exact number of characters. To find names containing exactly six characters: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname REGEXP '^......$';The pattern contains: ^ ...... $where: ^ means beginning of the string. Each . represents one character. $ means end of the string. Therefore: ^......$means: The complete string must contain exactly six characters.

The complete pattern: ^.{6}$means: Beginning ↓ Any character repeated exactly 6 times ↓ End

content: Module 1: Sorting Data with ORDER BY When retrieving data using a SELECT statement, rows are not guaranteed to appear in a particular order unless an explicit sorting rule is specified. The ORDER BY clause is used to organize the rows returned by a query.
title: Sorting Data and Working with NULL in MySQL (Lecture 06)

content: 1.1 General Syntax The basic syntax is: SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name ORDER BY column_name;The ORDER BY clause specifies the column that should be used to sort the result.
title: Sorting Data and Working with NULL in MySQL (Lecture 06)

content: 1.2 Ascending Sort Ascending order is the default sorting direction. For example, to display students’ first names and birth dates ordered from the earliest birth date to the latest: mysql> SELECT fname, birth_date -> FROM students -> ORDER BY birth_date;Example output: +---------------+------------+ | fname | birth_date | +---------------+------------+ | Mohan | 1990-01-01 | | Rukzana | 1990-03-06 | | Yuhatharshana | 1990-05-07 | | Thuvarakan | 1990-11-10 | | Mithujan | 1990-12-09 | | Malith | 1991-03-02 | | Utpala | 1992-04-12 | | Barath | 1992-05-04 | | Shirmal | 1993-02-08 | | Darmarathna | 1993-05-05 | +---------------+------------+ 10 rows in set (0.00 sec)The query: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students ORDER BY birth_date;sorts the records according to birth_date in ascending order. Important: ASC is the default sorting direction, so it does not have to be written explicitly.
title: Sorting Data and Working with NULL in MySQL (Lecture 06)

content: Module 2: Ascending Sorting with ASC Although ascending order is the default, you can explicitly specify it using the ASC keyword. SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students ORDER BY birth_date ASC;This produces the same ordering as: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students ORDER BY birth_date;
title: Sorting Data and Working with NULL in MySQL (Lecture 06)

content: Meaning of ASC ASC means: Ascending order For numerical values, ascending means smallest to largest. For dates, ascending means earliest to latest. For text, ascending generally means alphabetical order.
title: Sorting Data and Working with NULL in MySQL (Lecture 06)

content: Examples Numerical values: 10 20 30 40 50Dates: 1990-01-01 1991-03-02 1992-04-12 1993-05-05Names: Barath Malith Mohan Rukzana

content: Module 3: Descending Sorting with DESC To sort results in reverse order, use the DESC keyword. DESC means: Descending order For example: mysql> SELECT fname, birth_date -> FROM students -> ORDER BY birth_date DESC;Example output: +---------------+------------+ | fname | birth_date | +---------------+------------+ | Darmarathna | 1993-05-05 | | Shirmal | 1993-02-08 | | Barath | 1992-05-04 | | Utpala | 1992-04-12 | | Malith | 1991-03-02 | | Mithujan | 1990-12-09 | | Thuvarakan | 1990-11-10 | | Yuhatharshana | 1990-05-07 | | Rukzana | 1990-03-06 | | Mohan | 1990-01-01 | +---------------+------------+ 10 rows in set (0.00 sec)The query: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students ORDER BY birth_date DESC;returns the latest birth date first and the earliest birth date last.

Similarly, do not use: != NULLor: <> NULLto test whether a value is not NULL.

content: Module 1: The Anatomy of the SELECT Statement The SELECT statement is the primary SQL command used to retrieve information from a database table.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 1.1 General Query Syntax The basic structure of a SELECT statement is: SELECT what_to_select FROM which_table WHERE conditions_to_satisfy;A basic SELECT statement consists of three main parts: Clause Purpose SELECT Specifies which columns should be retrieved FROM Specifies the table from which data is retrieved WHERE Specifies conditions used to filter rows Important: The WHERE clause is optional. If it is omitted, all rows from the selected table are returned.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Module 2: Selecting All Data (*) To retrieve every column and every row from a table, use the asterisk (*) wildcard.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 2.1 Basic SELECT * Query mysql> SELECT * FROM students;This query retrieves the complete dataset stored in the students table. The * symbol means: All columns For example: SELECT * FROM students;returns every column for every row in the students table.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Module 3: Selecting Particular Rows (WHERE Clause) Instead of retrieving every row, you can filter records using the WHERE clause. The general syntax is: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition;The condition determines which rows are included in the result.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 3.1 Filtering by Exact Match (=) To find a specific student whose first name is Barath: mysql> SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname = "Barath";Equivalent formatted query: SELECT * FROM students WHERE fname = "Barath";The = operator checks whether the value stored in the fname column is equal to "Barath".
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 3.2 Using Comparison Operators (>=) To find students born on or after January 1, 1991: mysql> SELECT * FROM students WHERE birth_date >= "1991-01-01";Equivalent formatted query: SELECT * FROM students WHERE birth_date >= "1991-01-01";The >= operator means: Greater than or equal to
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Common Comparison Operators Operator Meaning = Equal to > Greater than < Less than >= Greater than or equal to <= Less than or equal to <> Not equal to
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Module 4: Combining Conditions with Logical Operators SQL allows multiple conditions to be combined using logical operators. The two fundamental logical operators covered in this lecture are: AND OR
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 4.1 Combining Conditions with AND The AND operator is used when all specified conditions must be true. For example, to find female students belonging to the PHY department: mysql> SELECT * FROM students WHERE dept = "PHY" AND sex = "f";Equivalent formatted query: SELECT * FROM students WHERE dept = "PHY" AND sex = "f";A row is returned only when both conditions are satisfied: dept = "PHY" AND sex = "f"AND requires every connected condition to be true.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 4.2 Combining Conditions with OR The OR operator is used when at least one condition must be true. For example, to find female students or students belonging to the COM department: mysql> SELECT * FROM students WHERE sex = "f" OR dept = "COM";Equivalent formatted query: SELECT * FROM students WHERE sex = "f" OR dept = "COM";A row is returned when either condition is true, or when both conditions are true. OR requires at least one connected condition to be true.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 4.3 AND vs OR Operator Requirement AND All conditions must be true OR At least one condition must be true
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Module 5: Selecting Particular Columns (Column Projection) Sometimes you do not want to retrieve every column from a table. Instead, you can specify only the columns that you need. This is called column projection.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 5.1 Selecting Specific Columns For example: mysql> SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students;Equivalent formatted query: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students;Only the fname and birth_date columns are returned.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 5.2 Selecting Multiple Columns Multiple columns are separated using commas: SELECT fname, lname, dept FROM students;Another example: SELECT index_no, fname, birth_date FROM students;
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: 5.3 Projection vs SELECT * Using: SELECT * FROM students;retrieves all columns. Using: SELECT fname, birth_date FROM students;retrieves only the selected columns. Projection controls which columns appear in the result.
title: Mastering SQL SELECT Statements & Filtering (SQL Part 05)

content: Method 1: Using the INSERT Statement To insert a single record manually: INSERT INTO students VALUES ( '12/BMS/01', 'Samantha', 'Bandara', '12, Main Street, Kurunagela', 'm', '1999-03-05', 'BMS', 'TCEUSL', NULL );
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Understanding the INSERT Statement The values are inserted according to the order in which the columns were defined in the students table. The example contains: Column Value index_no 12/BMS/01 fname Samantha lname Bandara address 12, Main Street, Kurunagela sex m birth_date 1999-03-05 dept BMS campus TCEUSL tp_no NULL
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Method 2: Loading Data from a Text File (LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE) For bulk insertion, you can create a text file such as students.txt. Each line represents one record, and values are separated by tabs in the order of the table columns. Example: 12/BMS/01 Samantha Bandara 12, Main Street, Kurunagela m 1999-03-05 BMS TCEUSL NULL 12/BMS/02 Kamal Perera 25, Lake Road, Colombo m 1998-07-12 BMS TCEUSL 0712345678The general command for loading the data is: mysql> LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE "C:/wamp64/bin/mysql/mysql5.7.14/data/students.txt" -> INTO TABLE students;Important: The exact file path depends on where your text file is stored. Windows paths can be written using forward slashes in MySQL commands, such as C:/folder/file.txt.
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Module 5: Understanding Common Data Types The students table uses several important MySQL data types.
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: VARCHAR VARCHAR(n) stores variable-length character strings. Example: fname VARCHAR(20)This allows a name with up to 20 characters.
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: CHAR CHAR(n) stores fixed-length character strings. Example: sex CHAR(1)This is suitable for a single character such as: mor: f
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: DATE DATE stores date values. Example: birth_date DATEA typical value is: 1999-03-05The standard MySQL date format is: YYYY-MM-DD
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Module 6: Understanding SHOW TABLES After selecting a database, use: SHOW TABLES;This command displays all tables available in the currently selected database. Example: mysql> USE tceusl; Database changed mysql> SHOW TABLES; +------------------+ | Tables_in_tceusl | +------------------+ | students | +------------------+ 1 row in set (0.02 sec)If there are no tables: Empty set
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Module 7: Understanding DESCRIBE The DESCRIBE command is used to inspect the structure of a table. Syntax: DESCRIBE table_name;Example: DESCRIBE students;It provides information such as: Field name Data type Whether NULL is allowed Key information Default value Extra attributes Example: +------------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+ | Field | Type | Null | Key | Default | Extra | +------------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+ | index_no | varchar(20) | YES | | NULL | | | fname | varchar(20) | YES | | NULL | | | lname | varchar(20) | YES | | NULL | | | address | varchar(30) | YES | | NULL | | | sex | char(1) | YES | | NULL | | | birth_date | date | YES | | NULL | | | dept | varchar(5) | YES | | NULL | | | campus | varchar(5) | YES | | NULL | | | tp_no | varchar(15) | YES | | NULL | | +------------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Module 8: Understanding DROP TABLE The DROP TABLE statement permanently removes a table from the selected database. Syntax: DROP TABLE table_name;Example: DROP TABLE students;After executing the command: SHOW TABLES;may produce: Empty setImportant: DROP TABLE removes both the table structure and its data. Always confirm that the table is no longer required before executing this command.
title: Creating and Using Databases & Tables in MySQL (SQL Part 04)

content: Module 9: Complete Practical Workflow The complete process for creating and populating the students table is: 1. Start WAMP/XAMPP 2. Start MySQL 3. Open the MySQL Console 4. Login using the configured credentials 5. View available databases 6. Create a new database 7. Select the database 8. Check existing tables 9. Create the students table 10. Verify the table using SHOW TABLES 11. Inspect the structure using DESCRIBE 12. Insert records using INSERT 13. Load bulk records using LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 14. Verify the stored data 15. Drop the table only when it is no longer requiredExample: SHOW DATABASES; CREATE DATABASE tceusl; USE tceusl; SHOW TABLES; CREATE TABLE students ( index_no VARCHAR(20), fname VARCHAR(20), lname VARCHAR(20), address VARCHAR(30), sex CHAR(1), birth_date DATE, dept VARCHAR(5), campus VARCHAR(5), tp_no VARCHAR(15) ); SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE students; INSERT INTO students VALUES ( '12/BMS/01', 'Samantha', 'Bandara', '12, Main Street, Kurunagela', 'm', '1999-03-05', 'BMS', 'TCEUSL', NULL );

content: 3.1 Syntax Rules and Case Sensitivity Semicolon Termination: Most MySQL statements must end with a semicolon (;) or \g. The MySQL client uses the terminator to determine when a statement is complete rather than simply using the end of a line. Case Insensitivity: SQL keywords are generally case-insensitive. The following queries are equivalent: mysql> SELECT VERSION(), CURRENT_DATE; mysql> select version(), current_date; mysql> SeLeCt vErSiOn(), current_DATE;
title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

content: 3.2 Example 1: Checking Version and Current Date mysql> SELECT VERSION(), CURRENT_DATE; +-----------+--------------+ | VERSION() | CURRENT_DATE | +-----------+--------------+ | 5.7.14 | 2016-11-14 | +-----------+--------------+ 1 row in set (0.07 sec)Output Information MySQL returns information about the query result, including the number of rows returned and the execution time. Note: The exact version, date, and execution time displayed on your system will depend on your MySQL installation and the current date.
title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

content: 3.3 Example 2: Using MySQL as a Calculator You can perform mathematical operations and invoke functions directly in the MySQL query monitor: mysql> SELECT SIN(PI()/4), (4+1)*5; +--------------------+-------------+ | SIN(PI()/4) | (4+1)*5 | +--------------------+-------------+ | 0.7071067811865476 | 25 | +--------------------+-------------+ 1 row in set (0.07 sec)This demonstrates that MySQL can evaluate mathematical expressions and built-in functions without requiring a table.
title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

content: 3.4 Example 3: Multiple Statements on a Single Line You can execute multiple queries on one line when the MySQL client configuration permits multiple statements, with each statement ending with its own semicolon. Example: mysql> SELECT VERSION(); SELECT NOW(); +-----------+ | VERSION() | +-----------+ | 5.7.14 | +-----------+ 1 row in set (0.00 sec) +---------------------+ | NOW() | +---------------------+ | 2016-11-14 21:22:19 | +---------------------+ 1 row in set (0.00 sec)Important: In some client environments or application APIs, multiple statements may be disabled or require explicit configuration. The interactive MySQL monitor can process separate statements entered sequentially.
title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

content: 4.1 Writing Multi-Line Statements Because MySQL uses the semicolon (;) to determine statement boundaries rather than line breaks, a single query can span multiple lines. Example: mysql> SELECT -> USER(), -> CURRENT_DATE; +----------------+--------------+ | USER() | CURRENT_DATE | +----------------+--------------+ | root@localhost | 2016-11-14 | +----------------+--------------+ 1 row in set (0.05 sec)Note: The -> prompt indicates that MySQL is waiting for you to complete the current statement.
title: Introduction to MySQL (SQL Part 03)

content: 4.2 Canceling an In-Progress Command (\c) If you make a mistake while typing a query or decide to abandon a multi-line statement before executing it, you can cancel the current statement by typing \c. Example: mysql> SELECT -> USER() -> \c mysql>The \c command clears the current unfinished statement and returns you to the normal mysql> prompt.

content: 2.2 Authentication Password Prompt: When the console opens: c:\wamp64\bin\mysql\mysql5.7.14\bin\mysql.exeit will display: Enter password:Default Login: By default in standard local development installs, there may be no password set for the root user. If the root account has no password, simply press the Enter key to bypass the prompt. Security Note: Never assume that the root account has a blank password on every installation. Production and secured development environments should use a strong password and appropriate user privileges.

content: Module 7: Understanding SQL Command Termination In the MySQL console, SQL statements are normally terminated using a semicolon: SHOW DATABASES;The semicolon tells the MySQL client that the current SQL statement has ended. The \g command can also be used to execute the current statement: SHOW DATABASES\gIf the semicolon is omitted, the MySQL console may continue waiting for additional input. For example: mysql> SELECT * -> FROM students -> WHERE id = 1;The -> prompt indicates that MySQL is waiting for the remainder of the statement.
title: Managing Databases Using MySQL in Local Servers  (SQL Part 02)

content: Module 8: Understanding the MySQL Prompt When the MySQL console is ready to receive a command, you will normally see: mysql>Example: mysql> SHOW DATABASES;If a statement is incomplete, the prompt can change to: ->For example: mysql> SELECT * -> FROM students -> WHERE id = 1;

content: Cancelling an Incomplete Statement Use: \cExample: mysql> SELECT * -> FROM students -> \c mysql>This clears the current unfinished SQL statement.

content: 1.1 What is an Environment Stack? Local development stacks bundle an operating system, web server, database management system, and scripting language together. WAMP: Specifically tailored for Windows environments: W — Windows A — Apache M — MySQL P — PHP XAMPP: A cross-platform development environment: X — Cross-platform A — Apache M — MySQL/MariaDB P — PHP P — Perl XAMPP can be used across Windows, Linux, and macOS.
title: Comprehensive Study Guide: Installing, Configuring, and Testing XAMPP & MySQL (SQL Part 01)

content: 1.2 Core Component Breakdown 1. Apache HTTP Server (httpd) Acts as the core web server software. Receives incoming HTTP requests from web browsers. Processes and serves web resources back to clients over the network. Commonly listens on Port 80 for HTTP traffic and Port 443 for HTTPS traffic. 2. MySQL / MariaDB A Relational Database Management System (RDBMS). Stores structured application data. Uses Structured Query Language (SQL). Can store: User accounts Product information Transactions Customer records Application settings Other structured data 3. PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) A server-side scripting language designed for web development. Executes on the web server rather than directly in the user’s browser. Can communicate with databases such as MySQL/MariaDB. Dynamically generates HTML output that is returned to the client browser.

content: Module 3: Service Management and Operations A local server environment depends on background services or processes. Apache and MySQL must be running before applications that depend on them can operate correctly.

content: 3.1 Managing Services Using WAMP Server WAMP Server provides a notification-area icon that indicates the status of its services. Finding the WAMP Icon Look for the WAMP icon in the Windows Notification Area/System Tray, normally located at the bottom-right of the taskbar. The icon may indicate different service states. Typical meanings: Red: Services are stopped or unavailable. Orange: Some services are running while others are stopped. Green: Required services are running correctly. Starting All Services Click the WAMP notification-area icon. Select Start All Services. Wait for Apache and MySQL to start. Verify that the indicator becomes green. Stopping All Services Click the WAMP notification-area icon. Select Stop All Services. Apache and MySQL will be stopped. Network ports and system resources used by the services will be released. Restarting All Services If configuration files or PHP extensions are modified: Open the WAMP menu. Select Restart All Services. Wait for the services to stop and start again. Verify that the services return to the expected state.
title: Comprehensive Study Guide: Installing, Configuring, and Testing XAMPP & MySQL (SQL Part 01)

content: 3.2 Managing Services Using the XAMPP Control Panel Open the: XAMPP Control PanelThe panel provides controls for individual server modules. Starting Apache Locate Apache in the module list. Click Start. The Apache process should start. The PID and Port information should appear. The Apache row should indicate that it is running. Starting MySQL Locate MySQL in the module list. Click Start. Wait for the database server to initialize. Verify that MySQL is running. Stopping a Service Click Stop next to the corresponding service. For example: Apache → Stop MySQL → StopRestarting a Service Stop the required service and then click Start again. This can be useful after configuration changes.

content: Module 7: Basic Architecture of a PHP + MySQL Application A typical local PHP/MySQL application works approximately as follows: User | | HTTP Request v Web Browser | v Apache Web Server | v PHP Application | | SQL Query v MySQL / MariaDB | | Database Result v PHP Application | | Generated HTML v Apache | v Web Browser

content: Request Flow The user enters a URL in the browser. The browser sends an HTTP request. Apache receives the request. Apache identifies the requested PHP file. PHP executes the application logic. PHP communicates with MySQL/MariaDB if database information is required. MySQL processes the SQL query. The database returns the requested data. PHP generates the response. Apache sends the response back to the browser. The browser displays the resulting webpage.
